find-the-index-of-the-first-occurrence-i.pattern: String matching: naive scan → Rabin–Karp rolling hash → KMP prefix function

approaches.name: Check every start position
approaches.idea: For each position in `haystack` where `needle` could fit, compare character by character.
steps: For `i` from 0 to `n − m`: compare `haystack[i + j]` with `needle[j]` for `j = 0..m − 1`.
Return `i` on the first full match; −1 if none.
approaches.why: Up to n − m + 1 starts, each comparing up to m characters (e.g. "aaaa…ab" in "aaaa…a").

approaches.name: Rabin–Karp rolling hash
approaches.idea: Hash the needle, then slide a window of length m over the haystack, updating its hash in O(1) per step (drop the leftmost character, add the new one). Only compare characters when the hashes match.
steps: Polynomial hash with base 131 modulo 10⁹ + 7; precompute `high = 131^(m−1)`.
For each `i`: if the window is full, subtract `haystack[i − m]·high`; then `h = h·131 + haystack[i]`.
When `h` equals the needle's hash, confirm with a direct comparison and return the start.
approaches.why: O(n + m) expected; a hash collision costs an extra O(m) check, so adversarial inputs could degrade it — which KMP avoids.

approaches.name: KMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt)
approaches.idea: Precompute, for every prefix of the needle, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix (`pi`). On a mismatch, jump to `pi[j − 1]` instead of restarting — the haystack pointer never moves back.
steps: Build `pi` for `needle`: for each `i`, fall back `k = pi[k − 1]` while `needle[i] != needle[k]`; extend `k` on a match.
Scan `haystack` with `j` = matched length, falling back the same way on mismatches.
When `j == m`, return `i − m + 1`.
approaches.why: Guaranteed linear: each fall-back undoes an earlier extension, so total work is bounded by n + m.

rotate-string.pattern: Every rotation of s is a substring of s + s

approaches.name: Try every rotation
approaches.idea: Build each of the n rotations of `s` and compare it with `goal`.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false.
For each `k` from 0 to n − 1: if `s[k..] + s[..k]` equals `goal`, return true.
approaches.why: n rotations, each built and compared in O(n).

approaches.name: Search for goal inside s + s
approaches.idea: Writing `s` twice in a row contains every rotation as a length-n window. So `goal` is a rotation exactly when the lengths match and `goal` occurs in `s + s`.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false.
Otherwise return whether `s + s` contains `goal`.
approaches.why: One line, but the library search is the naive O(n·m) scan in the worst case.

approaches.name: KMP search in s + s
approaches.idea: Same observation, with a guaranteed-linear search: build the KMP prefix function of `goal` and scan `s + s` with it.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false.
Build `pi` for `goal`.
Scan `s + s`, falling back with `pi` on mismatches; return true when a full match is found.
approaches.why: Linear in the 3n characters involved, no matter the input.

repeated-substring-pattern.pattern: KMP prefix function: the smallest period is n − pi[n − 1]

approaches.name: Try every block length that divides n
approaches.idea: A repeating block must have a length `L` that divides n and is at most n/2. For each such `L`, check that every character equals the one `L` positions earlier.
steps: For `L` from 1 to n/2 with `n % L == 0`:
If `s[i] == s[i − L]` for all `i ≥ L`, return true.
Return false.
approaches.why: d(n) = number of divisors of n (at most 64 for n ≤ 10⁴), each checked in O(n).

approaches.name: Look for s inside (s + s) without its ends
approaches.idea: If `s` is a repetition, rotating it by one block gives `s` again, so `s` occurs in `s + s` at some position other than 0 and n. Removing the first and last character of `s + s` rules those two out.
steps: Let `t = (s + s)` with its first and last characters removed.
Return whether `t` contains `s`.
approaches.why: Elegant, but the library substring search is O(n·m) in the worst case.

approaches.name: Period from the KMP prefix function
approaches.idea: `p = pi[n − 1]` is the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, so `n − p` is the smallest period of `s`. The string is a whole-number repetition exactly when `p > 0` and that period divides n.
steps: Build the prefix function `pi` of `s`.
Let `p = pi[n − 1]`.
Return `p > 0 && n % (n − p) == 0`.
approaches.why: One linear pass to build `pi`.

repeated-string-match.pattern: Bound the repetitions (⌈|b|/|a|⌉ or one more), then string-search with KMP

approaches.name: Keep appending a and searching
approaches.idea: Append `a` one copy at a time and check whether `b` appears yet. Any match fits within ⌈|b|/|a|⌉ + 1 copies (it can start anywhere inside the first copy), so stop after that.
steps: Let `limit = |b| / |a| + 2`.
For `k` from 1 to `limit`: append `a`; if the string contains `b`, return `k`.
Return −1.
approaches.why: Up to m/n + 2 library searches, each O(length · m) in the worst case.

approaches.name: One KMP search over ⌈m/n⌉ + 1 copies
approaches.idea: Build `t` = `a` repeated `q + 1` times, where `q = ⌈|b|/|a|⌉`. Find the first occurrence of `b` in `t` with KMP; the copies needed are those covering up to the end of that occurrence.
steps: `q = ⌈m / n⌉`; `t = a` repeated `q + 1` times.
KMP-search `b` in `t`; if not found, return −1.
With first match ending at index `end` (exclusive), return `⌈end / n⌉`.
approaches.why: `t` has at most m + 2n characters and KMP is linear. The first occurrence ends earliest, so it needs the fewest copies.

repeated-dna-sequences.pattern: Fixed-size sliding window + hashing (2 bits per letter → 20-bit rolling code)

approaches.name: Compare each window with every later window
approaches.idea: For each 10-letter window, look for an identical window later in the string; collect matches in a set so each answer appears once.
steps: For each start `i`, compare `s[i..i+10)` with `s[j..j+10)` for every `j > i`.
On a match, add the window to a result set and stop scanning for this `i`.
approaches.why: About n²/2 window comparisons of 10 letters each.

approaches.name: Hash set of windows
approaches.idea: Slide over every 10-letter window, storing seen windows in a set. A window seen before goes into the answer set.
steps: For each start `i`: `w = s[i..i+10)`.
If `w` is already in `seen`, add it to `repeated`; otherwise add it to `seen`.
Return `repeated`.
approaches.why: L = 10: each window is copied and hashed as a 10-character string.

approaches.name: 2-bit rolling code
approaches.idea: With only four letters, each fits in 2 bits, so a 10-letter window is a 20-bit integer. Slide it in O(1): shift left by 2, add the new letter, mask to 20 bits. Track counts per code in a 2²⁰ table.
steps: Map A, C, G, T to 0, 1, 2, 3.
For each `i`: `code = ((code << 2) | val(s[i])) & (2²⁰ − 1)`.
Once `i ≥ 9`, increment `count[code]`; when it becomes exactly 2, add `s[i − 9..i]` to the answer.
approaches.why: O(1) per step with no string hashing; the table has 4¹⁰ ≈ 10⁶ entries regardless of n. Adding at count 2 reports each sequence once.

longest-happy-prefix.pattern: KMP prefix function: pi[n − 1] is the longest border

approaches.name: Try every length, longest first
approaches.idea: For `L` from n − 1 down to 1, compare the prefix and suffix of length `L`; the first match is the answer.
steps: For `L` from n − 1 down to 1: if `s[0..L) == s[n−L..n)`, return that prefix.
Return "".
approaches.why: Up to n lengths, each compared in O(L).

approaches.name: Rolling hash of prefix and suffix
approaches.idea: Grow the prefix one character at the end and the suffix one character at the front, updating both polynomial hashes in O(1). Remember the longest length where they agree.
steps: Prefix hash: `hp = hp·B + s[L − 1]`. Suffix hash: `hs = s[n − L]·B^(L−1) + hs`.
Use two moduli (10⁹ + 7 and 10⁹ + 9) to make collisions negligible.
Track the largest `L < n` with equal hashes and return `s[0..L)`.
approaches.why: Linear, but probabilistic: a double-hash collision is astronomically unlikely, not impossible. KMP gives the same bound deterministically.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def longestPrefix(self, s: str) -> str:
        M1, M2, B = 10**9 + 7, 10**9 + 9, 131
        n, best = len(s), 0
        p1 = p2 = s1 = s2 = 0
        w1 = w2 = 1
        for L in range(1, n):
            a, b = ord(s[L - 1]), ord(s[n - L])
            p1, p2 = (p1 * B + a) % M1, (p2 * B + a) % M2
            s1, s2 = (b * w1 + s1) % M1, (b * w2 + s2) % M2
            w1, w2 = w1 * B % M1, w2 * B % M2
            if p1 == s1 and p2 == s2:
                best = L
        return s[:best]

approaches.name: KMP prefix function
approaches.idea: `pi[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `s[0..i]` that is also its suffix. For the whole string that is exactly the happy prefix: `pi[n − 1]`.
steps: Build `pi`: for each `i`, fall back `k = pi[k − 1]` while `s[i] != s[k]`; extend `k` on a match.
Return `s[0..pi[n − 1])`.
approaches.why: Deterministic linear time: total fall-backs never exceed total extensions.

shortest-palindrome.pattern: Longest palindromic prefix via KMP on s + "#" + reverse(s)

approaches.name: Find the longest palindromic prefix directly
approaches.idea: The answer keeps the longest palindromic prefix of `s` in the middle and mirrors the rest in front. Test prefixes from longest to shortest.
steps: For `end` from n down to 1: if `s[0..end)` is a palindrome (two pointers), stop.
Return `reverse(s[end..])` + `s` (for an empty string, return "").
approaches.why: Up to n prefixes, each palindrome check O(n) — e.g. "aaa…ab".

approaches.name: Forward and backward rolling hashes
approaches.idea: A prefix is a palindrome when it reads the same both ways. Maintain its hash read forwards (`h·B + c`) and backwards (`c·B^i + h`) as it grows; equal hashes mean a palindrome.
steps: For `i` from 0 to n − 1, update both hashes with `s[i]` (two moduli to avoid collisions).
When they agree, record `end = i + 1`.
Return `reverse(s[end..]) + s`.
approaches.why: O(1) per character; correct with overwhelming probability (double hashing), whereas KMP is exact.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def shortestPalindrome(self, s: str) -> str:
        M1, M2, B = 10**9 + 7, 10**9 + 9, 131
        f1 = f2 = b1 = b2 = 0
        w1 = w2 = 1
        end = 0
        for i, ch in enumerate(s):
            c = ord(ch)
            f1, f2 = (f1 * B + c) % M1, (f2 * B + c) % M2
            b1, b2 = (c * w1 + b1) % M1, (c * w2 + b2) % M2
            w1, w2 = w1 * B % M1, w2 * B % M2
            if f1 == b1 and f2 == b2:
                end = i + 1
        return s[end:][::-1] + s

approaches.name: KMP on s + "#" + reverse(s)
approaches.idea: A palindromic prefix of `s` equals a suffix of `reverse(s)`. In `t = s + "#" + reverse(s)`, the last prefix-function value is the longest prefix of `s` that matches a suffix of `reverse(s)` — the longest palindromic prefix. The `#` stops matches running past `s`.
steps: Build `t = s + "#" + reverse(s)` and its prefix function `pi`.
`L = pi[last]` is the longest palindromic prefix length.
Return `reverse(s)[0..n − L) + s`.
approaches.why: One deterministic linear pass over 2n + 1 characters.

longest-duplicate-substring.pattern: Binary search on the answer length + Rabin–Karp rolling hash

approaches.name: Every length, longest first, with a set of substrings
approaches.idea: For each length `L` from n − 1 down to 1, put every substring of length `L` in a set; the first repeat found is a longest duplicate.
steps: For `L` from n − 1 down to 1: for each start, add `s[i..i+L)` to a set.
If it was already there, return it.
Return "" if no length repeats.
approaches.why: Up to n lengths × n substrings × O(L) to build and hash each.

approaches.name: Binary search on the length, with a set of substrings
approaches.idea: If some substring of length `L` repeats, so does one of length `L − 1` (drop its last letter). That monotonicity lets you binary-search the largest repeating `L`, testing each candidate with a set of substrings.
steps: `dup(L)`: return the start of a repeated length-`L` substring (using a set), or −1.
If `dup(mid)` succeeds, record it and search longer; otherwise search shorter.
approaches.why: log n checks, each building n substrings of length up to n.

approaches.name: Binary search + Rabin–Karp
approaches.idea: Same binary search, but test a length in O(n) with a rolling hash: slide a window, update its hash in O(1), and look it up in a hash map of starts. Confirm a hash hit by comparing the actual characters.
steps: Binary search the length as before.
`dup(L)`: hash the first window (two moduli), then roll: `h = h·B + s[i] − s[i − L]·B^L`.
If the combined hash was seen before and the two substrings really match, return the current start.
approaches.why: log n checks of O(n) each (character checks only on hash hits). Two moduli keep false hits negligible, and the direct check means a false hit can never produce a wrong answer.
